terms.comment: The ordinary word. Labrum superius, the upper lip; labrum īnferius, the lower (Traupman). Not lābrum, a basin.
The diminutive, of a baby’s lips; in Plautus a pet name too (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: lip; mostly in the plural, labia
terms.comment: Ante- and post-classical for labrum (Lewis & Short): Plautus’s and Terence’s feminine labea, Pliny’s neuter plural labia, and so in Church Latin.

phrases.latin: Torquātus volō parvulus mātris ē gremiō suae porrigēns tenerās manūs dulce rīdeat ad patrem sēmihiante labellō
phrases.english: I want a little Torquatus, reaching out his tender hands from his mother’s lap, to laugh sweetly at his father with half-open lips

phrases.latin: Platōnī cum in cūnīs parvulō dormientī apēs in labellīs cōnsēdissent
phrases.english: when Plato was a baby asleep in his cradle and bees settled on his little lips

phrases.latin: Domine, labia mea aperiēs, et ōs meum annūntiābit laudem tuam.
phrases.english: Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.

labrum.html: Hor. C. 1.13.12, dente labrīs notam, the close of a lesser asclepiad: la- takes a short place; Vergil makes the syllable heavy before br (E. 3.43, necdum illīs labra admōvī). De Vaan 319, s.v. labium. Lābrum, a basin, is another word, from lavābrum (de Vaan 330).

sources: Lewis & Short: labrum · Lewis & Short: labellum · Lewis & Short: labia
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 319, s.v. labium, and p. 330, s.v. lavō.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 58, 340.
Caesar, Horace, Vergil, Cicero and Catullus checked against the Latin Library text (CLTK mirror); Pliny and the psalm from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-plinius, loci-vulgata).
